subject: Peschel et al. (2025)
object: Peschel et al. (2025) reported a previously undescribed IRF6 variant that caused a new type of ectodermal dysplasia with natal teeth.

subject: Zhang et al. (2026)
object: Zhang et al. (2026) reported that gain-of-function variants in the IRF6 gene cause a syndrome of hidradenitis suppurativa, ectodermal dysplasia, and deafness.

subject: Schneider et al. (2026)
object: Schneider et al. (2026) described 2 unrelated male teenagers (P1, aged 17, and P2, aged 14) with ectodermal dysplasia who were born with natal teeth. P1 developed 7 deciduous teeth with delay and 12 permanent teeth (10 remaining), most with enamel defects and hypomineralization, and had a highly atrophic mandibular alveolar crest due to oligodontia; P2 developed only 9 permanent teeth. Both had overheating since infancy, anhidrosis with no sweat glands detectable on the palms, recurrent skin abscesses in the genital/gluteal area, behind the ears, axillae and mouth, very dry skin with plantar hyperkeratosis and blistering of the toes in winter, dysplastic thickened nails with distal onycholysis, thick nasal mucus, dry cerumen, and bilateral sensorineural hearing impairment since infancy; submucous cleft palate was excluded.

subject: Schneider et al. (2026)
object: In P1 and P2, 2 unrelated males with ectodermal dysplasia with natal teeth, Schneider et al. (2026) identified the same de novo heterozygous c.653T>A transition in exon 6 of the IRF6 gene, resulting in an ile218-to-asn (I218N) substitution, by exome sequencing (P1) and Sanger sequencing (P2, after negative EDA, EDAR, EDARADD and TP63 testing). The variant was absent from parental DNA and was predicted to be deleterious.

subject: Schneider et al. (2026)
object: Schneider et al. (2026) described a 22-year-old woman (P3) with anhidrosis, diffuse xerosis, dilated follicular ostia, heat intolerance, recurrent hidradenitis suppurativa-like abscesses of the groins, axillae and intergluteal fold, pincer nails of both great toes, bilateral acquired sensorineural hearing loss, epistaxis, crusted rhinitis, insufficient salivation, and bilateral superficial punctate keratitis with reduced tear film break-up time. Hair, lips, palate, breasts and nipples were normal and natal teeth were not remembered; she had 16 persisting deciduous teeth and only 2 permanent teeth after delayed eruption.

subject: Schneider et al. (2026)
object: In P3, Schneider et al. (2026) identified a de novo heterozygous c.658T>C transition in the IRF6 gene, resulting in a ser220-to-pro (S220P) substitution, by trio whole-genome sequencing; a variant allele frequency of 30.5% indicated mosaicism. In silico analyses supported pathogenicity, though the variant was formally classified as of unknown significance.

subject: Schneider et al. (2026)
object: Comparing their 3 patients with 2 previously reported patients carrying IRF6 Ile218Asn or Ile218_Ser220delins variants, Schneider et al. (2026) considered oligodontia, hypo- or anhidrosis, hidradenitis suppurativa-like abscesses, poikiloderma, onychodysplasia and bilateral hearing impairment to be syndrome-defining (5/5), whereas natal teeth (2/5) and sparse hair (2/5) were irregular; none had lip pits, clefting, pterygia or syndactyly, distinguishing the disorder from VWS1 and PPS.

subject: Schneider et al. (2026)
object: Schneider et al. (2026) recognized a common pattern of tooth agenesis in P1, P2 and P3: all had permanent upper incisors but no mandibular incisors or canines and no permanent premolars, with pronounced atrophy of the lower alveolar crest.

subject: Schneider et al. (2026)
object: Schneider et al. (2026) found focal subcorneal clefting, basal spongiosis and absent sweat glands in skin biopsies from P1 and P3; keratinocyte nuclei of P1 showed stronger IRF6 immunostaining than controls, while P3 showed patchy nuclear staining consistent with mosaicism, and keratin 17 staining was normal. Together with genotype-phenotype data, they suggested a gain-of-function mechanism; AlphaFold3 modeling placed both substitutions in a short alpha-helix at the end of the region between the DNA-binding and protein-binding domains.

subject: Schneider et al. (2026)
object: Schneider et al. (2026) noted that they initially referred to this disorder as ectodermal dysplasia with natal teeth (EDNAT), but that natal teeth appeared less typical than initially thought.
